newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU COMMISSIONER OPPOSES EMU STABILITY PACT DELAY.
newsitem.headline: EU COMMISSIONER OPPOSES EMU STABILITY PACT DELAY.

text.p: The European Union commissioner for monetary affairs called on EU leaders on Tuesday to agree a pact for the single currency at their summit next week despite a request for more time from France's new left-wing government.

Commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy said the EU needed to stick by the agreed schedule if the single European currency were to be credible. "There must be an agreement now...The road to the single currency needs a clear view," he told France Inter radio.
"Sticking to the schedule is important, otherwise we will signal a backtracking that would be very harmful for everyone, particularly for France," said de Silguy, himself a Frenchman.
French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn threw plans for European economic and monetary union (EMU) into confusion on Monday.
At a meeting of EU finance ministers in Luxembourg he asked for time to study a previously agreed "stability pact" to keep budget deficits tight after EMU is launched.
The pact, agreed after hard-fought negotiations in Dublin in December, is supposed to be ratified by EU leaders when they meet in Amsterdam next week.
EMU is supposed to be well down the agenda at Amsterdam, where EU leaders want to focus on internal reforms before the recruitment of new members from post-communist Europe early in the next century.
But the EMU issue is likely to be prominent at the June 16-17 summit, which is unusually being held being held on weekdays when financial markest are open rather than the usual weekend arrangement.
Financial markets are sensitive to any suggestion that EMU might be launched on schedule in 1999 as countries struggle to reach the targets, notably in cutting budget deficits, for entry.

The issue is likely to dominate talks in Paris on Tuesday afternoon between Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok -- the Netherlands currently holds the rotating EU presidency -- and French President Jacques Chirac.
Chirac, a right-winger, has been forced to "cohabitate" with the centre-left after the Socialists took power following elections earlier this month.

A meeting of centre-right European leaders in Strasbourg on Tuesday is also likely to focus on EMU. It will be attended by Chancellor Helmut Kohl, whose coalition has been rocked by disputes over how Germany should qualify for EMU.

France's European Affairs Minister Pierre Moscovici insisted on Tuesday that Paris needed more than a week to study the EU stability pact, an integral part EMU, and carry out an audit of state finances.
"If we request an assessment, it means it will take a bit more than one week," he told RMC radio.

Moscovici said it was only normal that Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, who took office last week and is to outline his policy on June 19, be given time to study texts that were approved before he came to office.

"We will see from an audit of state finances what is our room for manoeuvre," Moscovici said. "My conviction is that the state finances are not healthy. The audit will reveal this and from there we will have to work out a realistic budget."
He said the budget would include Jospin's campaign pledge to create 700,000 jobs for young people to curb record 12.8 percent unemployment.
Moscovici said the EU would need to take into account the change in the bloc's political balance after the coming to power of the Labour party in Britain and the left in France.
"Social democrats have a majority, it is up to them to discuss and define a joint conception and convince the others," he said.

"We do not intend to start a crisis. We are here so that Europe moves forward, but also so that our European friends take our national priorities into account. Moving towards Europe without undoing France was our campaign slogan and this slogan will be the government's line," he said.
